Capability score by model, on the selected 15-task view

Not a raw pass rate. The solid bar is Projected — the value shown and ranked by — a best-guess estimate for each untested task, built from that task's typical pass rate across every model, adjusted by how much this specific model has over- or under-performed on the tasks it HAS been tested on (that adjustment is itself distrusted until there's enough tested evidence to back it, so a model with only a couple of tested tasks projects close to the plain typical rate rather than confidently extrapolating a small sample). The thin gray bracket under the bar is the honest range it was chosen from: Proven (assumes every untested task fails) to Max (assumes every untested task passes) — both shown as their own columns on the right, along with how many tasks were actually Failed and Tested. All three collapse to one number once a model reaches full 15/15 coverage — at that point the bar is just the real, fully-known score, with no projection involved. Repeat runs of the same task are folded into one estimate per (model, task) pair, shrunk toward that task's own typical pass rate across every model — not toward a 50/50 coin flip, so a task tried only once isn't penalized just for lacking repeats. Tasks are weighted by how much they distinguish models and how consistent repeat runs on them are, so a hard, reliably model-splitting task counts for more than one everybody handles the same way. Ties are broken by average tries-to-pass. The main model's other 210 tasks aren't included here — see its full-run figure in the stat row above.

Generation speed on passing runs

Completion tokens per second of wall-clock time, averaged over each model's passing shortlist runs. Duration and token counts both include every internal retry within a run, so this cancels out most of the "more tries = more work" effect — it's throughput, not luck.

Tokens generated per passing run

Tokens per pass, normalized to each exercise's own difficulty — 1.0× is the average token cost among models that passed that exercise, so a model that mostly solved cheap exercises isn't flattered and one that solved expensive ones (like clock, ~2.4× the shortlist average) isn't unfairly penalized. All three panels share one column order, so you can see whether a model's token cost, wall-clock cost, and retry cost all tell the same story. Each faint dot is one passing run; the bold dot per model is the average, connected to trace the trend. Tries taken is jittered slightly to keep identical values from stacking into one dot.

Quality vs. token cost

Each point is a model: projected capability score (the same estimate as the chart above) on the selected 15-task view against average tokens per pass, normalized to exercise difficulty (same 1.0× = typical basis as the chart above). Top-left is the efficiency sweet spot — high score for cheap; bottom-right is the model to cut. Bubble size is passing-run count.

Pass / fail by task × model

Rows ranked top-to-bottom by task quality (discriminative power, rewarded; cost and inconsistency, penalized — same composite as the "quality" column below). Columns ranked left-to-right by the option below (default: average tokens generated, cheapest model first). Green = passed (majority of runs, for tasks re-run more than once), shaded by how many tries it took on average — dark green means it passed fast, pale green means it barely scraped by. Red = failed. A cell that's been re-run and landed some of each way — neither a clean pass nor a clean fail — gets a diagonal hatch so it doesn't read as identical to a clean result at a glance; the pass/total number underneath (shown whenever a task was attempted more than once) is the exact split. A small dot in the corner flags a cell with at least one run that hit the harness's max-duration limit rather than failing on its own — hover for exactly which run(s) and how many of the cell's failures were timeouts; a task with a high timeout share among its failures may just need a longer duration budget rather than reflecting real model inconsistency (see Timeout rate in the usefulness table below).

Exercise usefulness — is this task worth keeping?

Each of the 15 currently selected tasks with surviving data, plotted by cost (average wall-clock time, all models) against how much it splits the model field (0 = every model landed the same way, pass or fail; 1 = an even 50/50 split — the most information a task can give). A task voided entirely (e.g. by a harness bug) is left off rather than shown as a false 0/0. Bubble size is attempt count; color is which way the split leans. Cheap + high-split (top-left) is the best-value task; expensive + low-split (bottom-right) is the prime candidate to cut. The table's Quality column folds discriminative power, cost, and flakiness into one number (higher = better) — it's what orders the heatmap's rows above. Score weight is a related but distinct number — discriminative power × reliability, cost excluded — it's how much this task counts toward the "Capability score by model" chart above. Flakiness is shrunk toward the typical (usually low) flakiness across every other exercise, weighted by how many models actually re-ran this one — a task re-run by exactly one model that split 1/2 isn't treated as confidently "maximally flaky" the way one re-run by seven models with a consistent mixed result is. Timeout rate is what fraction of this task's failures were the harness bailing on its max-duration limit rather than the model actually failing on its own (count in parentheses) — unlike Flakiness, this isn't folded into Quality or Score weight, since a model that reliably always times out on a task is consistent, not flaky; a high rate here is a hint the duration budget may be too tight for this specific task, worth checking before reading too much into its other numbers.

Pass vs. fail cost, per exercise

Every attempt at each shortlist exercise — passes in green, fails in red — showing how much work got burned whether or not it landed. The bold dots are the pass/fail averages; the dashed line is the gap between them. Tokens and duration share one column order (sorted by the token gap, biggest first) so the two panels compare directly — a mismatch between them (e.g. a big token gap but a small time gap) means passes and fails take a similar amount of wall-clock time despite very different token counts, often a sign of throttling or a slow non-generation step.

Tries taken before the run ended, across all models

Most passes land by try 2–3. Try 6 was the retry ceiling for most configs — the runs that reach it are almost entirely failures that never converged before the budget ran out.
